prompt: Which unit could be used for the **area** of a netball court?

feedback.b: Metres measure length, such as the perimeter of the court.
feedback.d: km/h is a unit of speed.

hints: Area is measured by counting squares.
solution: Area is measured in **square** units, such as **m²**.

prompt: What is the name of a quadrilateral that has **exactly one** pair of parallel sides?
hints: Its area formula is $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$.
solution: A **trapezium**. (In the USA it is called a trapezoid.)

prompt: Which calculation gives the area of this triangle?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 310 242" width="310" height="242" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="14"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#ffffff"/><polygon points="40,190 278,190 142,54" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="142" y1="54" x2="142" y2="190" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polyline points="152,190 152,180 142,180" fill="none" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="159" y="206.2" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">14 cm</text><text x="66.84" y="103.88" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">10 cm</text><text x="163.68" y="122" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#2563eb">8 cm</text><text x="300" y="230" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Not to scale</text></svg>
figure.alt: A triangle with a base of 14 cm, a sloping side of 10 cm, and a dashed perpendicular height of 8 cm.

feedback.b: 10 cm is a sloping side, not the perpendicular height.
feedback.c: This is the area of the rectangle around the triangle. The triangle is half of it.
feedback.d: The base is 14 cm. The 10 cm side is not at right angles to the 8 cm height.

hints: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × perpendicular height.
The perpendicular height meets the base at a right angle.
solution: Base 14 cm, perpendicular height 8 cm: $\frac{1}{2} \times 14 \times 8 = 56$ cm². The 10 cm side is not needed.

prompt: Match each shape to its area formula.
hints: The kite formula uses its two diagonals.
The trapezium formula uses its two parallel sides.
solution: Rectangle $l \times w$; triangle $\frac{1}{2}bh$; parallelogram $bh$; trapezium $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$; kite $\frac{1}{2}d_1 d_2$.

prompt: Select **all** the shapes that have an area of exactly 24 cm². (All heights are perpendicular heights.)

options.text: A triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm
A parallelogram with base 8 cm and height 3 cm
A trapezium with parallel sides 5 cm and 7 cm, and height 4 cm
A kite with diagonals 4 cm and 6 cm

hints: Work out each area separately.
Remember the ½ in the triangle, trapezium and kite formulas.
solution: Rectangle: $6 \times 4 = 24$ ✓. Triangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 4 = 12$ ✗. Parallelogram: $8 \times 3 = 24$ ✓. Trapezium: $\frac{1}{2} \times (5 + 7) \times 4 = 24$ ✓. Kite: $\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 6 = 12$ ✗.

prompt: Explain why the area of a parallelogram is base × perpendicular height, and not base × the length of the slanted side.
modelAnswer: If you cut the triangle off one end of the parallelogram and move it to the other end, the parallelogram becomes a rectangle. The rectangle has the same base, and its height is the perpendicular height of the parallelogram (not the slanted side). So the area is base × perpendicular height. The slanted side is longer than the height, so using it would give too big an answer.

rubric.criterion: Describes cutting off a triangle and moving it to make a rectangle with the same area
States that the rectangle's height is the perpendicular height, so area = base × perpendicular height (the slanted side is longer and gives too much)

hints: Imagine cutting a triangle off one end of the parallelogram and sliding it to the other end. What shape do you get?
solution: Cutting a triangle from one end and moving it to the other turns the parallelogram into a rectangle with the same base and the same perpendicular height, so $A = b \times h$. The slanted side is longer than the height, so it would give too large an area.

prompt: A rectangle has the same area as a triangle with base 18 cm and perpendicular height 10 cm. The rectangle is 6 cm wide. How long is the rectangle?
hints: Find the area of the triangle first.
Then length × 6 = that area.
solution:
Triangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 10 = 90$ cm².

Rectangle: $l \times 6 = 90$, so $l = 90 \div 6 = 15$ cm.

prompt: The base and the perpendicular height of a triangle are **both doubled**. What happens to its area?

feedback.b: Doubling just one of the lengths would double the area. Here both are doubled.
feedback.c: The triangle is bigger in both directions, so its area must grow.
feedback.d: Only two lengths are multiplied together for an area, so it's 2 × 2, not 2 × 2 × 2.

hints: Try it with numbers: base 4 and height 6, then base 8 and height 12.
solution: New area $= \frac{1}{2} \times (2b) \times (2h) = 4 \times \frac{1}{2}bh$. The area is **multiplied by 4**. For example, base 4, height 6 gives 12; base 8, height 12 gives 48.

prompt: A garden bed is a trapezium. Its parallel sides are 14 m and 9 m, and they are 6 m apart. A square paved area, 3 m by 3 m, sits inside the bed. The rest of the bed will be covered with bark that costs \$12 per square metre. How much will the bark cost?
hints: Find the area of the trapezium, then subtract the paved square.
Multiply the area that needs bark by \$12.
solution:
Trapezium: $\frac{1}{2} \times (14 + 9) \times 6 = 69$ m².

Paved square: $3 \times 3 = 9$ m².

Bark area: $69 - 9 = 60$ m². Cost: $60 \times 12 = 720$, so the bark costs **\$720**.

stem: A rectangular swimming pool is 25 m long and 12 m wide. A concrete path 2 m wide goes all the way around the outside of the pool, as shown.
prompt: How long is the **outside** edge of the path, along the long side of the pool?

hints: The path sticks out 2 m beyond the pool at **both** ends.
solution: $25 + 2 + 2 = 29$ m. (In the same way, the outside width is $12 + 2 + 2 = 16$ m.)

stem: A rectangular swimming pool is 25 m long and 12 m wide. A concrete path 2 m wide goes all the way around the outside of the pool, as shown.
prompt: Find the area of the path.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 380 218" width="380" height="218" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="14"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#ffffff"/><rect x="45" y="30" width="290" height="160" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="65" y="50" width="250" height="120" fill="#bfdbfe" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><text x="190" y="110" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1e3a8a">Pool</text><text x="190" y="64" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">25 m</text><text x="88" y="110" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">12 m</text><line x1="315" y1="110" x2="335" y2="110" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="1.2"/><line x1="315" y1="115" x2="315" y2="105" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="1.2"/><line x1="335" y1="115" x2="335" y2="105" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="0" y="0" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"></text><text x="354" y="110" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">2 m</text><text x="190" y="40" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="11" fill="#4b5563">path</text><text x="372" y="210" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Not to scale</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rectangular pool 25 m long and 12 m wide, with a path 2 m wide all the way around it. The outside edge of the path is a larger rectangle.

hints: Area of the path = area of the outside rectangle − area of the pool.
The outside rectangle is 4 m longer and 4 m wider than the pool.
solution:
Outside rectangle: $29 \times 16 = 464$ m². Pool: $25 \times 12 = 300$ m².

Path $= 464 - 300 = 164$ m².

stem: A rectangular swimming pool is 25 m long and 12 m wide. A concrete path 2 m wide goes all the way around the outside of the pool, as shown.
prompt: Tia finds the area of the path by multiplying the perimeter of the pool by the width of the path: $2 \times (25 + 12) \times 2 = 148$ m². Explain why Tia's answer is too small, and give the correct area.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 380 218" width="380" height="218" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="14"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#ffffff"/><rect x="45" y="30" width="290" height="160" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="65" y="50" width="250" height="120" fill="#bfdbfe" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><text x="190" y="110" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1e3a8a">Pool</text><text x="190" y="64" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">25 m</text><text x="88" y="110" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">12 m</text><line x1="315" y1="110" x2="335" y2="110" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="1.2"/><line x1="315" y1="115" x2="315" y2="105" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="1.2"/><line x1="335" y1="115" x2="335" y2="105" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="0" y="0" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"></text><text x="354" y="110" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">2 m</text><text x="190" y="40" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="11" fill="#4b5563">path</text><text x="372" y="210" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Not to scale</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rectangular pool 25 m long and 12 m wide, with a path 2 m wide all the way around it. The outside edge of the path is a larger rectangle.

modelAnswer: Tia's method covers four strips along the sides of the pool: two strips 25 m by 2 m and two strips 12 m by 2 m, which is 148 m². But it misses the four square corners of the path, each 2 m by 2 m = 4 m². Adding these gives 148 + 4 × 4 = 164 m².

rubric.criterion: Explains that her method only covers the strips along the four sides of the pool and misses the four corner squares
Shows the corners add 4 × (2 × 2) = 16 m², giving the correct area of 164 m²

hints: Sketch the four strips that Tia has counted. Which parts of the path are left over?
solution: Tia's calculation counts a strip along each side of the pool: $2 \times 25 \times 2 + 2 \times 12 \times 2 = 100 + 48 = 148$ m². It leaves out the **four corner squares**, each $2 \times 2 = 4$ m². Correct area $= 148 + 16 = 164$ m².

prompt: Find the area of the triangle part of the wall.

The base of the triangle is the full width of the wall.

stem: The end wall of a bach is a rectangle 8 m wide and 3 m high, with a triangle on top. The top of the triangle is 2 m above the top of the rectangle. The wall has a window 1.5 m wide and 1.2 m high, and a door 0.9 m wide and 2 m high.
prompt: The wall will be painted, but not the window or the door. Find the area that will be painted.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 222" width="340" height="222" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="14"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#ffffff"/><polygon points="50,190 290,190 290,100 170,40 50,100" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="100" x2="290" y2="100" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="170" y1="100" x2="170" y2="40" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polyline points="170,91 179,91 179,100" fill="none" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="186" y="76" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">2 m</text><rect x="80" y="118" width="45" height="36" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="102.5" y="136" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2937">window</text><rect x="200" y="130" width="27" height="60" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="213.5" y="160" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2937">door</text><text x="170" y="207" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">8 m</text><text x="308" y="145" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">3 m</text></svg>

hints: Find the area of the whole wall (rectangle + triangle) first.
Then subtract the area of the window and the area of the door.
solution:
Rectangle: $8 \times 3 = 24$ m². Triangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 2 = 8$ m². Whole wall: $24 + 8 = 32$ m².

Window: $1.5 \times 1.2 = 1.8$ m². Door: $0.9 \times 2 = 1.8$ m².

Painted area $= 32 - 1.8 - 1.8 = 28.4$ m².

stem: The end wall of a bach is a rectangle 8 m wide and 3 m high, with a triangle on top. The top of the triangle is 2 m above the top of the rectangle. The wall has a window 1.5 m wide and 1.2 m high, and a door 0.9 m wide and 2 m high.
prompt: The wall (not the window or the door) needs **two** coats of paint. One litre of paint covers 12 m², and the paint is sold in 2-litre tins. How many tins must be bought?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 222" width="340" height="222" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="14"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#ffffff"/><polygon points="50,190 290,190 290,100 170,40 50,100" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="100" x2="290" y2="100" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="170" y1="100" x2="170" y2="40" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polyline points="170,91 179,91 179,100" fill="none" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="186" y="76" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">2 m</text><rect x="80" y="118" width="45" height="36" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="102.5" y="136" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2937">window</text><rect x="200" y="130" width="27" height="60" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="213.5" y="160" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2937">door</text><text x="170" y="207" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">8 m</text><text x="308" y="145" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937">3 m</text></svg>

hints: Find the area to be painted, then double it for two coats.
Work out how many litres are needed, then how many 2-litre tins that takes. You can't buy part of a tin.
solution:
Area to paint: $32 - 1.8 - 1.8 = 28.4$ m². Two coats: $2 \times 28.4 = 56.8$ m².

Paint needed: $56.8 \div 12 = 4.73\ldots$ litres.

Two tins hold only 4 L, which is not enough, so **3 tins** (6 L) must be bought.

prompt: A square has an area of 49 cm². How long is each side?

feedback.b: 12.25 is 49 ÷ 4. Dividing by 4 finds the side from the **perimeter**, not the area.
feedback.c: 24.5 is 49 ÷ 2. The area of a square is side × side, so look for a number times itself.
feedback.d: A square with 49 cm sides would have an area of 49 × 49 = 2401 cm².

hints: Area of a square = side × side.
Which number times itself makes 49?
solution: Side × side = 49, and $7 \times 7 = 49$, so each side is **7 cm**.

prompt: In area formulas, the height must be the **perpendicular** height. This means it meets the base at [[a]].
hints: Perpendicular lines meet like the corner of a page.
solution: The perpendicular height meets the base at **a right angle** (90°). A sloping side is not the height.

prompt: A trapezium has parallel sides of 6 cm and 10 cm, and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Leo types $6 + 10 \times 4 \div 2$ into his calculator and gets 26 cm². What has gone wrong?

options.text: He should multiply all three: $6 \times 10 \times 4 \div 2 = 120$ cm²

feedback.b: The trapezium formula is $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$, so you do halve.
feedback.c: The parallel sides are **added**, not multiplied: $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$.
feedback.d: The calculator worked out $10 \times 4 \div 2$ first and then added 6. The parallel sides must be added first.

hints: Which does a calculator do first: + or ×?
In $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$, the brackets mean the parallel sides are added first.
solution: The calculator follows the order of operations, so it worked out $6 + (10 \times 4 \div 2) = 6 + 20 = 26$. The parallel sides must be added first: $\frac{1}{2} \times (6 + 10) \times 4 = \frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 4 = 32$ cm².

prompt: A rectangular poster is 84 cm long and 60 cm wide. Find its area in **square metres** (m²).
hints: Change the lengths into metres first (100 cm = 1 m).
Or find the area in cm², then use 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
solution:
In metres the poster is 0.84 m by 0.6 m, so its area is $0.84 \times 0.6 = 0.504$ m².

(Or: $84 \times 60 = 5040$ cm², and $5040 \div 10\,000 = 0.504$ m².)

prompt: Lines ℓ and m are parallel. Triangles A, B and C each have a base of 4 cm on line m, and each has its top corner on line ℓ. Which statement is true?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 420 222" width="420" height="222" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="14"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="24" y1="50" x2="410" y2="50" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="24" y1="190" x2="410" y2="190" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="121.5,54.9 128.5,50 121.5,45.1" fill="none" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.8"/><polyline points="131.5,194.9 138.5,190 131.5,185.1" fill="none" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="12" y="50" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2937">ℓ</text><text x="12" y="190" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2937">m</text><polygon points="36,190 116,190 36,50" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="36,180 46,180 46,190" fill="none" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="60" y="150" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937" font-weight="bold">A</text><text x="76" y="206" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">4 cm</text><polygon points="166,190 246,190 206,50" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><text x="206" y="150" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937" font-weight="bold">B</text><text x="206" y="206" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">4 cm</text><polygon points="286,190 366,190 404,50" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><text x="350" y="150" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937" font-weight="bold">C</text><text x="326" y="206" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">4 cm</text></svg>
figure.alt: Two parallel lines, ℓ at the top and m at the bottom. Three triangles A, B and C each have a 4 cm base on line m and a top corner on line ℓ. A is right-angled, B is symmetrical, and C leans far over to the right.

options.text: All three triangles have the same area
C has the largest area, because it has the longest sides
A has the largest area, because it has a right angle
You need the lengths of the sloping sides to compare them

feedback.b: Long sloping sides don't make a bigger area. Area depends on the base and the **perpendicular** height.
feedback.c: The right angle doesn't make the area bigger. All three have the same base and the same perpendicular height.
feedback.d: The sloping sides aren't needed. The perpendicular height of each triangle is the distance between the parallel lines.

hints: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × perpendicular height.
What is the perpendicular height of each triangle?
solution: Each triangle has a 4 cm base, and its perpendicular height is the distance between the parallel lines, which is the same for all three. So every area is $\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times h$: **all three have the same area**, even though they look different.

prompt: Explain how two copies of the same trapezium can be fitted together to show that the area of a trapezium is $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$, where $a$ and $b$ are the parallel sides and $h$ is the perpendicular height.
modelAnswer: Take two identical trapeziums and turn one upside down (rotate it 180°). Put them side by side so they fit together. They make a parallelogram. The base of the parallelogram is a + b (the bottom of one trapezium plus the bottom of the upside-down one), and its perpendicular height is still h. So the parallelogram's area is (a + b) × h. Each trapezium is half of the parallelogram, so its area is ½(a + b)h.

How much of each small square is inside the shaded square?
solution: Joining the midpoints of opposite sides cuts the large square into 4 equal small squares. Each side of the shaded square is a diagonal of one small square, and a diagonal cuts a square exactly in half. prompt: A trapezium has an area of 60 cm² and a perpendicular height of 6 cm. One of its parallel sides is 4 cm longer than the other. How long is the **shorter** parallel side?
hints: Call the shorter side $a$. Then the longer side is $a + 4$.
Use $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h = 60$ with $b = a + 4$ and $h = 6$, then solve for $a$.
solution:
Let the shorter side be $a$ cm, so the longer side is $(a + 4)$ cm.

$\frac{1}{2} \times (a + a + 4) \times 6 = 60$

$3(2a + 4) = 60$, so $2a + 4 = 20$, $2a = 16$ and $a = 8$ cm.

Check: sides 8 cm and 12 cm give $\frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 6 = 60$ ✓
